items.question_text: Will Dan S. Sullivan publicly concede Alaska's 2026 U.S. Senate race by November 27, 2026?
items.background_info:
Alaska's November 3, 2026 U.S. Senate election is the last Senate contest in the country still uncalled (Mississippi was called for Democrat Scott Colom). As of the Alaska Division of Elections' unofficial summary report timed 12 November 2026, the first-choice tally was: Mary Peltola (D) 125,157 (49.08%), Dan S. Sullivan (R, incumbent) 119,357 (46.80%), Gerald Heikes (R) 5,490 (2.15%), Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 4,199 (1.65%) and write-in 807 (0.32%), with roughly 257,000 ballots cast of 605,433 registered voters. Tens of thousands of absentee ballots were still being tallied in mid-November. The 15-day count, which includes ballots mailed from outside the U.S., closes on 18 November, when the Division conducts the official ranked-choice tabulation; the Division's calendar gives 25 November 2026 as its target date for certifying the election.

Because no candidate is near 50%, the race will be decided by ranked-choice transfers from Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Independent analyses of the Division's cast-vote records — the Alaska Beacon and Anchorage Daily News ran the RCTab software, and the New York Times did its own analysis — have found that Senator Sullivan gains on transfers but not by enough to erase Peltola's first-choice lead, and that more of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.'s voters rank Peltola ahead of Senator Sullivan. Peltola's campaign manager, Cheryl Bruce, has said the campaign is "exceptionally confident" of winning once transfers are applied. On that basis Peltola is widely regarded as the favourite, but the margin is small enough that the 18 November tabulation is the decisive event.

Neither candidate had conceded as of 13 November. Sullivan said on 11 November: "With tens of thousands of ballots still to be counted, there's a long way to go before every Alaskan's voice is heard." Before the election he said he would honour the outcome. Senate orientation for new members began in the week of 9 November. A concession is voluntary: nothing in Alaska law requires one, it has no effect on the count, and a narrowly beaten candidate has reasons to wait for certification or to keep the recount and contest windows open.

The result is also entangled in litigation. The Trump administration's Justice Department sued on 22 October to bar Alaska from certifying the Senate result if Sullivan loses, arguing that voters were confused by two Sullivans on the ballot. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit on 1 November for lack of standing, and DOJ appealed to the Ninth Circuit (No. 26-7304), where the briefing schedule runs to 14 December (DOJ) and 11 January 2027 (answering briefs); voting-rights intervenors moved for summary affirmance on 9 November, and DOJ has not sought an injunction pending appeal. A separate DOJ criminal investigation continues, and the Peltola campaign's own suit seeking the names of rejected absentee voters was dismissed by an Anchorage Superior Court judge on 11 November. After certification, recount requests are due within five days of the State Review Board's completion (28 November for governor, 30 November for other offices) and election contests by 5 December, so a losing campaign can keep fighting well past the count. Unofficial results are published at https://www.elections.alaska.gov/enr/26GENR/results/ElectionSummaryReportRPT.pdf and litigation is tracked at https://www.democracydocket.com/cases/alaska-u-s-senate-election-certification-challenge-doj.

items.resolution_criteria: This question resolves YES if Dan S. Sullivan — the Republican incumbent U.S. Senator for Alaska — publicly concedes defeat in Alaska's 2026 U.S. Senate election at any time by 11:59 p.m. UTC on November 27, 2026, and NO otherwise (including if Sullivan is instead certified as the election's winner). A qualifying concession is a public statement by Sullivan himself, or by his campaign or an authorised spokesperson on his behalf, acknowledging that he has lost the election and/or that Mary Peltola (or any other rival candidate) has won it. Statements that only note that ballots are still being counted, that the campaign is awaiting final results or certification, or that decline to comment do not qualify. Resolution will be based on [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).
items.fine_print: A concession that is later retracted, or that is followed by a recount request or an election contest, still counts. A hedged or conditional acknowledgment (for example, congratulating Peltola "if these results hold") does not qualify unless and until Sullivan states that he has lost. A concession reported second-hand (for example, the Peltola campaign saying Sullivan called to congratulate her) counts only if Sullivan or his campaign confirms it.
